Each record is the registry entry and plan row for one unit; the shipping commit registers it in src/data/puzzles.js, writes the plan row to docs/OVERNIGHT-PLAN.md, bumps livePuzzles, and removes the record. Delete this file when it is empty.

units.oneLiner: Give each vertex the smallest color its colored neighbors have not used, taking the vertices in the order that is hardest to fool: the one whose neighbors already show the most distinct colors goes next, ties broken by the most uncolored neighbors; one pass, at most one more color than the largest degree, and exactly two on any bipartite graph.
units.description: Greedy graph coloring with the DSatur saturation order against an exact branch-and-bound chromatic number on 200 random graphs of 24 vertices: optimal on 129 of 200 (average excess 0.355 colors) against 98 for recursive largest first, 58 for smallest-last, 56 for largest-first, and 18 for a random order; exactly 2 colors on 200 of 200 random bipartite graphs where largest-first needed up to 5; at n = 600, 18 and 75 colors against 20 and 80 for largest-first and 19 and 76 for RLF at a thirteenth to a thirty-sixth of RLF's neighbor scans; and the crown graph K50,50 minus a matching, where largest-first and RLF use 50 colors on a 2-colorable graph and DSatur uses 2.
units.time: O(n^2 + m) with a scan, O((n + m) log n) with a heap

units.plan_row: Greedy graph coloring × DSatur saturation ordering. Puzzle 168, graphs (problemSlug vertex-coloring, the atlas problem page carrying "Vertex coloring"). Solution greedy_graph_coloring_dsatur_saturation_ordering.py (0.7s, prints OK): the greedy pass with a scan counter, largest-first, smallest-last with degree buckets (reports degeneracy), DSatur, recursive largest first, Brelaz's exact branch and bound, random G(n, p), random connected bipartite graphs, the crown graph, and Mycielski's construction. ORACLES: (1) 200 random graphs n = 24, p in [0.2, 0.6], exact chi (8,207 search nodes total): optimal DSatur 129 / RLF 98 / smallest-last 58 / largest-first 56 / random 18 of 200, average excess 0.355 / 0.545 / 0.845 / 0.825 / 1.430; (2) every coloring proper, every greedy at most Delta + 1, smallest-last at most degeneracy + 1, DSatur exactly 2 on 200 of 200 random bipartite graphs (largest-first up to 5), Mycielski M3 / M4 / M5 chi 3 / 4 / 5 recovered by the exact solver and hit by every method; (3) G(600, 0.1): clique bound 4, Delta + 1 = 89, DSatur 18 colors (216,282 scans), RLF 19 (2,601,807), largest-first 20 (35,982), smallest-last 21 (71,964), random 22; G(600, 0.5): clique 10, Delta + 1 = 335, DSatur 75 (359,644), RLF 76 (12,832,354), largest-first 80 (179,344), smallest-last 81 (358,688), random 85; (4) crown graph K50,50 minus a matching: largest-first 50, RLF 50, smallest-last 2, DSatur 2. Honest: DSatur is wrong by a color on 71 of 200 small graphs, and the viz's random cycles include ties with largest-first (seed 20261014 opens with 4 against 5 at chi 4; seed 20261010 would have opened with a one-color loss, so the seed was chosen by a scan and the page says the order is not always better); author correction recorded (the draft hedged that RLF would use the fewest colors on dense graphs; measured one behind DSatur on both instances, not generalized). Cards: self, Recursive largest first, Backtracking coloring, Smallest-last ordering (greedy, algoName Greedy graph coloring). neverUse: a static order on the crown graph. Figure: the six-plus-six crown graph colored by largest-first (6) and DSatur (2) beside bars of optimal hits of 200; cite Brelaz CACM 1979 DOI 10.1145/359094.359101, Welsh and Powell 1967, Matula and Beck 1983, Johnson 1974. Viz DsaturViz: the same graph colored one vertex per tick by DSatur (left) and largest-first (right), random 20-vertex graphs with the exact chi computed at scene start on even cycles and the 8+8 crown graph on odd cycles; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles, every coloring proper on every tick; stepMs 600, holdTicks rests. Preserved narration: Aoede + Algieba.

units.oneLiner: Walk each query term's postings and add idf times a term frequency that saturates, tf (k1 + 1) / (tf + k1 (1 - b + b |d| / avgdl)), so the fifth occurrence of a word is worth far less than the first, two different query words beat one word twice, and a document ten times longer is not ten times more relevant.
units.description: BM25 with a saturating term frequency on a generated corpus whose relevance is known by construction (3,000 documents from 40 overlapping topics plus 40 keyword-stuffed documents, 200 queries of two or three words): mean average precision 0.897 and precision at ten 0.992 against 0.706 for tf-idf summation, 0.874 for cosine, 0.822 for Dirichlet query likelihood, 0.788 for Boolean overlap, and 0.684 for raw counts; both ablations worse (0.855 without length normalization, 0.820 without saturation); the weight curve 1.000, 1.375, 1.774, 2.075, 2.187 at tf 1, 2, 5, 20, 200 against the ceiling 2.2; and a document repeating one query word 300 times at rank one on 67 of 200 queries under raw counts (5.9x the best genuine score) against none under BM25 (0.49x).
units.time: one postings walk per query term
units.space: the inverted index plus a length per document

units.plan_row: BM25 ranking × Saturating term frequency. Puzzle 169, data-retrieval (problemSlug document-ranking, the atlas problem page carrying "Document ranking"). Solution bm25_ranking_saturating_term_frequency.py (0.8s, prints OK): a generative corpus (40 topics with 40 focus words each drawn from a shared vocabulary of 1,500, 55/45 focus-background mix, log-normal lengths 20 to 2,000, 3,000 documents), 200 two-or-three-word queries with relevance = generating topic, 40 one-word stuffed documents (300 repeats among filler), an inverted index, and eight rankers over the same 540 postings per query: BM25 (k1 1.2, b 0.75), BM25 b = 0, BM25 k1 = 1000, tf-idf summation, cosine over tf-idf vectors, Dirichlet query likelihood (mu 2000), Boolean overlap, raw tf. ORACLES: (1) MAP / P@10 / nDCG@10: BM25 0.897 / 0.992 / 0.992; b = 0 0.855 / 0.991 / 0.992; k1 = 1000 0.820 / 0.880 / 0.843; tf-idf 0.706 / 0.808 / 0.782; cosine 0.874 / 0.931 / 0.922; QL 0.822 / 0.952 / 0.943; Boolean 0.788 / 0.939 / 0.941; raw tf 0.684 / 0.796 / 0.771; (2) saturation curve at average length 1.000, 1.375, 1.774, 2.075, 2.187 for tf 1, 2, 5, 20, 200 against the ceiling 2.2 (99.4% at tf 200); the k1 = 1e9, b = 0 limit reproduces the raw-tf top ten on 496 of 496 single-term queries; (3) ablations both no higher than the hero; (4) stuffed documents at rank one, of 200 queries: BM25 0, b = 0 0, Boolean 0, cosine 17, QL 22, tf-idf 67, raw tf 67, k1 = 1000 67; stuffed score over the best genuine: BM25 0.49x, cosine 0.85x, raw tf 5.90x, tf-idf 5.69x, k1 = 1000 6.77x. Honest: cosine is close behind (0.874) and QL is principled; a document holding all query words at the ceiling still outranks a modest one (the weakness section says so); author correction recorded (the first draft's disjoint topics and all-word stuffing made the task too easy and let stuffed documents win legitimately under BM25, so corpus and attack were rebuilt). Cards: self, TF-IDF ranking, Vector space model, Query likelihood model (all algoName). neverUse: a ranker linear in the term count on a corpus anyone can write to. Figure: weight curves (raw tf, BM25 at average and 3x length, the 2.2 ceiling) beside bars of queries topped by a stuffed document; cite Okapi at TREC-3 1995, Robertson and Zaragoza FnTIR 2009 DOI 10.1561/1500000019. Viz Bm25Viz: a two-word query over nine seeded documents with one stuffed, scored one posting per tick in two columns (raw tf, BM25), each BM25 contribution checked against the (k1 + 1) idf ceiling and the stuffed document never on top under BM25; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles, 0 breaks; stepMs 650, holdTicks rests. Preserved narration: Aoede + Algieba.

units.oneLiner: Hedge the option with the stock and the stock's expected return drops out, so the price is the discounted expected payoff under a measure where the stock drifts at the risk-free rate; assume constant volatility and the terminal price is lognormal, so that expectation is two normal distribution functions, C = S N(d1) - K e^(-rT) N(d2), and every sensitivity is a formula too.
units.description: Black-Scholes closed-form pricing on S = 100, K = 100, r = 5%, sigma = 20%, T = 1: call 10.450584 and put 5.573526, the PDE residual under 4e-6 at twenty points, put-call parity to 1e-12, five Greeks matching central differences to five places; three numerical rivals converging on it (the CRR lattice 0.0005 off at 4,000 steps and 8,006,001 nodes, Crank-Nicolson 0.0006 off at 800 x 800, Monte Carlo 10.500 +/- 0.047 at 100,000 paths); implied volatility inverting to a flat 20% from the model's own prices but to a 24.7% to 13.9% skew from Heston stochastic-volatility prices, the smile a constant volatility cannot make; and the vanilla formula 7.9x too high on an up-and-out barrier call (10.451 against 1.320 +/- 0.017).
units.baseline: Monte Carlo with exact lognormal draws

units.plan_row: Black-Scholes × Closed-form European pricing. Puzzle 170, optimization-or (problemSlug option-pricing, the atlas problem page carrying "Option pricing"; sibling live lesson binomial-options-pricing-cox-ross-rubinstein-lattice, puzzle 135). Solution black_scholes_closed_form_european_pricing.py (2.8s, prints OK): the call and put formulas with expiry and zero-volatility limits, analytic Greeks, the CRR lattice, a Crank-Nicolson solver (Thomas algorithm, Dirichlet boundaries), Monte Carlo with exact lognormal draws and standard errors, Brent inversion for implied volatility, a Heston Monte Carlo pricing five strikes on shared paths, and a daily-monitored up-and-out barrier call by simulation. ORACLES (S 100, K 100, r 5%, sigma 20%, T 1): (1) call 10.450584, put 5.573526; PDE residual at most 4.2e-6 over 20 (S, T) points by central differences; limits at expiry, zero volatility, S -> 0 and S -> inf; (2) parity to 0; Greeks delta 0.63683, gamma 0.01876, vega 37.524, theta -6.414, rho 53.232 all matching central differences to 1e-4 relative; (3) CRR N = 100 / 1,000 / 4,000: 10.43061 / 10.44858 / 10.45008 (errors 0.01997 / 0.00200 / 0.00050; 5,151 / 501,501 / 8,006,001 nodes); Crank-Nicolson 200 x 200 10.44069 (0.00989; 40,401 points), 800 x 800 10.44997 (0.00062; 641,601); Monte Carlo 10^4 paths 10.43508 +/- 0.1461, 10^5 paths 10.50005 +/- 0.0467 (a one-sigma miss, reported); (4) implied vol round trip 3.5e-14 at strikes 60 to 140, flat 20% from model prices; Heston (20,000 paths, 100 steps, kappa 1.5, theta 0.04, xi 0.6, rho -0.7) prices invert to 24.7% (23.5 to 25.7) at K 80, 21.6% at 90, 18.6% at 100, 15.7% at 110, 13.9% (13.6 to 14.1) at 120; (5) up-and-out call, barrier 120, daily monitoring: 1.320 +/- 0.017 against the vanilla 10.451, 7.9x. Honest: the 10^5 Monte Carlo run landed one standard error off and the table says so; author correction recorded (Crank-Nicolson at 200 x 200 expected within a tenth of a cent, measured a cent because of the kink at the strike). Cards: self, Binomial options pricing (live lesson badge), Monte Carlo option pricing, Crank-Nicolson (all algoName). neverUse: the vanilla formula for a path-dependent contract. Figure: the call value curve over the payoff with the at-the-money value marked, beside implied volatility by strike (flat model line, Heston skew with two-sigma bars); cite Black and Scholes JPE 1973 DOI 10.1086/260062, Merton 1973, Heston 1993. Viz BlackScholesViz: 250 lognormal terminal draws per tick for 60 ticks into a histogram with the in-the-money region amber, the discounted mean with its two-sigma band against the closed-form line, and the price curve over the payoff; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles x 60 ticks, the estimate within four standard errors on every tick past 1,000 paths; stepMs 200, holdTicks rests. Preserved narration: Aoede + Algieba.

units.oneLiner: After every assignment, run a queue of arcs: delete from a variable every value with no supporting partner left in a neighbor, and whenever a domain shrinks requeue every arc into it; stop at a fixpoint or a wipeout, then branch only on what survives, so a dead end is found where it is created instead of twenty levels deeper.
units.description: Maintaining arc consistency with AC-3 on random binary CSPs (25 variables, domain 6, density 0.3) across the phase transition, every solution checked constraint by constraint and every finishing solver agreeing: at tightness 0.44 MAC with MRV refutes an instance in 6 nodes against 93 for forward checking and 9 for MAC with a static order while chronological backtracking exhausts 200,000 nodes on 9 of 12 instances; at 0.30, 33 against 102 and 184,620 (11 unfinished); the propagation is the cost (11,484 constraint checks against 2,231); AC-3 proven on 40 exhaustively enumerated instances (every survivor supported, idempotent, no solution value removed) and under its e d^3 bound; AC-3 alone solving the easy Sudoku with no search and MAC taking 291 nodes to forward checking's 498 on a hard one.
units.time: O(e d^3) propagation per search node
units.space: a domain per variable per level

units.plan_row: Maintaining arc consistency × AC-3 propagation. Puzzle 171, search-constraints-games (problemSlug constraint-satisfaction, the atlas problem page carrying "Constraint satisfaction"; sibling live lesson backtracking-mrv). Solution maintaining_arc_consistency_ac3_propagation.py (8.8s, prints OK): a binary CSP class with allowed-pair sets and a check counter, revise and AC-3 with a seen set, an arc-consistency checker, one Solver class (modes bt / fc / mac, orders static / mrv, node budget), the model-B random generator, exhaustive enumeration, and a Sudoku-to-CSP builder with Norvig's easy and hard puzzles. ORACLES: (1) 40 small instances (7 variables, domain 4): six solver variants agree with enumeration on every one; AC-3 leaves every survivor supported, is idempotent, never removes a solution value; one AC-3 run 1,670 checks against the 2 e d^3 bound 35,856 (e = 83); (2) the race, 25 variables, domain 6, density 0.3, 12 instances per tightness, budget 200,000, per-instance averages of nodes / checks: t 0.30 (12/12 sat) BT 184,620 / 443,326 (11 unfinished), FC+MRV 102 / 1,686, MAC static 41 / 10,457, MAC+MRV 33 / 7,227; t 0.36 (8/12) BT 200,004 (12 unf), FC 295 / 5,518, MAC static 72 / 39,560, MAC+MRV 40 / 20,319; t 0.40 (0/12) BT 200,004 (12 unf), FC 386 / 7,148, MAC static 91 / 61,207, MAC+MRV 26 / 20,206; t 0.44 BT 171,781 (9 unf), FC 93 / 2,231, MAC static 9 / 15,377, MAC+MRV 6 / 11,484; t 0.48 BT 163,807 (8 unf), FC 46 / 1,255, MAC static 4 / 9,673, MAC+MRV 3 / 8,540; t 0.54 BT 118,314 (4 unf), FC 29 / 861, MAC 0 / 2,857; (3) Sudoku: AC-3 alone solves the easy puzzle (11,356 checks); hard puzzle FC+MRV 498 nodes / 16,178 checks, MAC+MRV 291 / 168,988; (4) unsatisfiable instance 0 at 0.44: MAC refutes in 4 nodes, chronological backtracking exhausts 200,000. Honest: MAC loses the constraint-check column at every tightness (two to five times FC) and the hard Sudoku costs 10x the checks; two author corrections recorded (MAC expected to win checks; MRV inside plain backtracking is meaningless and was replaced by MAC with a static order). Cards: self, Forward checking, Backtracking search (live lesson badge via backtracking-mrv), Min-conflicts (all algoName). neverUse: chronological backtracking without propagation at the transition. Figure: log-scale nodes and checks per instance against tightness for four solvers with the satisfiable share shaded; cite Mackworth AIJ 1977 DOI 10.1016/0004-3702(77)90007-8, Sabin and Freuder ECAI 1994, Mackworth and Freuder 1985. Viz Ac3Viz: AC-3 on a seeded 8-variable, 4-value network, one arc revision per tick, pruned values struck red, requeued arcs counted, ending arc consistent or wiped out, the consistency property checked at the end; NODE-VERIFIED 24 cycles (up to 85 revisions), 0 breaks; stepMs 650, holdTicks rests. Preserved narration: Aoede + Algieba.

units.oneLiner: Keep every key in the slot array itself and, when the home slot is taken, probe the next slot and the next: the probes stay inside the cache line the first one fetched, Knuth's 1963 formulas say exactly what each load factor costs, and the price is clustering, which is why the table resizes before it is full and why the hash must scatter neighbors.
units.description: Open addressing with linear probing on a 65,536-slot table against Knuth's 1963 formulas (hits and misses within 1% at loads 0.25 to 0.7, within 8% at 0.9) and a Python set shadowing 1,200,000 mixed operations across six structures: at load 0.9 a hit costs 5.315 probes but 1.540 cache lines against 2.570 and 2.570 for double hashing and 2.450 and 2.450 for chaining; clusters of 715 slots and a probe variance of 277 where Robin Hood hashing keeps the same mean with variance 19.8; a miss at 5.864 probes under tombstones against 1.698 under backward-shift deletion after deleting half the keys; and a weak hash on consecutive keys costing 1,056 probes per hit against 8.3 for double hashing.
units.time: O(1) expected; (1 + 1/(1 - a)) / 2 probes per hit

units.plan_row: Open addressing × Linear probing. Puzzle 172, data-structures (problemSlug hash-collision-resolution, the atlas problem page carrying "Cache-friendly hashing"; sibling live lesson cuckoo-hashing-two-table-eviction-kicks). Solution open_addressing_linear_probing.py (3.0s, prints OK): linear probing with tombstone or backward-shift deletion and a rebuild at 85% live-plus-tombstones, quadratic probing (triangular offsets), double hashing (odd stride), separate chaining, Robin Hood, Fibonacci and weak hashes, a probe-and-cache-line counter (8 slots per 64-byte line, one line per chaining node). ORACLES: (1) Knuth 1963 at loads 0.25 / 0.5 / 0.7 / 0.8 / 0.9 / 0.95: hits 1.164 / 1.509 / 2.172 / 3.027 / 5.962 / 11.609 against 1.167 / 1.500 / 2.167 / 3.000 / 5.500 / 10.500, misses 1.397 / 2.510 / 5.971 / 12.655 / 50.434 / 205.639 against 1.389 / 2.500 / 6.056 / 13.000 / 50.500 / 200.500 (within 6% to 0.8, 20% beyond); (2) 1,200,000 mixed operations across six structures all matching a Python set, final sizes matching; (3) the race at load 0.9 (every key looked up, 5,000 misses): linear probing 5.315 probes/hit, 47.975/miss, 1.540 lines/hit, variance 277, max 612, longest cluster 715; Robin Hood 5.315 / 5.644 / 1.540 / 19.8 / 29; quadratic 2.850 / 12.055 / 1.951 / 16.2 / 92; double hashing 2.570 / 10.056 / 2.570 / 11.1 / 68; chaining 2.450 / 1.923 / 2.450 / 0.5 / 9; longest run by load 8 / 31 / 85 / 209 / 752 / 3,250; (4) deletion: fill to 0.7, delete half: tombstones 5.864 probes per miss (formula for 0.7: 6.056), backward shift 1.698 (formula for 0.35: 1.683); (5) weak hash (high bits) on 2,048 consecutive keys in 4,096 slots: linear probing 1,056 probes per hit, double hashing 8.3, chaining 402.8, strong hash 1.50. Honest: linear probing pays twice double hashing's probes at 0.9 and wins only on lines; the Robin Hood mean is identical to 1e-9 (the displacement total is invariant), asserted; three author notes recorded (quadratic vs double ordering; the first weak-hash experiment at 65,536 slots ran quadratic for ten minutes and was shrunk; a 5,000-key hit sample was replaced by every key after the early-inserted keys biased it). Cards: self, Hash table with chaining, Robin Hood hashing, Cuckoo hashing (live lesson badge) (all algoName). neverUse: linear probing with a hash that keeps neighbors neighbors. Figure: Knuth's hit and miss curves with the measured points beside bars of the longest run by load; cite Knuth 1963 / TAOCP 3 6.4, Amdahl et al. 1954, Pagh-Pagh-Ruzic STOC 2007 DOI 10.1145/1250790.1250839. Viz LinearProbingViz: a 64-slot table as eight cache lines filling to load 0.9, walked slots amber and touched lines outlined, the running average probes per insert against Knuth's expectation, every key checked reachable from its home each tick; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles x 21 ticks, 0 breaks; stepMs 500, holdTicks rests. Preserved narration: Aoede + Algieba.
